did_you_know.text: The Hebrew word tevah means a box or floating container, and in the Torah it appears mainly in two stories: Moses’ basket and Noah’s ark. In both cases, it protects a person on the water.
Moses’ sister is not named here, but later in the Torah she is identified as Miriam. Her initiative shows how even a young girl can influence the course of events.

The verse explains the name Moses through the Hebrew verb mashah, meaning “to draw out of the water.” Scholars also note that Egyptian has a name element meaning “born,” so the name may echo the Egyptian language as well.

Midian was probably a region in the northwestern Arabian Peninsula, east or southeast of the Gulf of Aqaba; its exact borders are uncertain. Moses thus moves from the center of Egyptian power to a remote desert region.

Drawing water and watering animals were essential daily tasks in the ancient world, since there were no faucets or pumps. A well was also an important meeting place for communities living in pasturelands.
The name Gershom is connected with the Hebrew word ger, describing someone living in a land that is not his homeland. The child’s name expresses Moses’ feeling of being a stranger in Midian.

Mentioning Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob connects Israel’s suffering with the promises made to the ancestors in Genesis. In the Bible, a covenant is not merely an agreement but a binding relationship lasting across generations.

In the Bible, the verb “to know” can mean more than having information; it can also describe deep attention and recognition of someone’s situation. The verse therefore emphasizes that God notices the Israelites’ suffering and responds to it.
